name: Mator
confidence_why: Helimski 1997, the only full description of this language extinct since the 1840s, states that the accent marks in Müller's and Pallas's eighteenth-century wordlists fluctuate so much that describing Mator stress remains a task for future research if it is possible at all, and Helimski 1993 had said the same while only tentatively reading the marks as mobile stress; no other work treats the question.

catalog_locator: §1.5.16 'Akzentzeichen und Betonung', p. 133 (p. 137 of the SZTE Contenta open copy, eprint 38757)
catalog_quote: 1.5.16. Akzentzeichen und Betonung. Alle mehrsilbigen Wörter in Muellers Aufzeichnungen sind akzentiert (der Unterschied zwischen den Akzentzeichen " ´ " und " ` " ist irrelevant: das erste wurde in nichtletzten Silben, das zweite in der letzten Silbe gebraucht). Auch bei Pallas ist die Wortbetonung häufig notiert. Die Schwankungen in der Notation sind jedoch so stark, daß selbst die Möglichkeit, diese akzentologischen Angaben zu benutzen, problematisch bleibt (vgl. z.B. 340 iləndä 'lebendig', belegt als TM MM ilínde, KM íllende, KP ilindé: dialektale Variation oder ganz einfach willkürliche Akzentuierung?). Deshalb bleibt die Beschreibung der Betonung in der matorischen Sprache - wenn eine solche Beschreibung überhaupt möglich ist - eine Aufgabe der zukünftigen Forschung.

new_statements.translation: All polysyllabic words in Mueller's records carry accent marks (...). Pallas, too, frequently notes word stress. The fluctuations in the notation are, however, so strong that even the possibility of using these accentological data remains problematic (cf. e.g. 340 iləndä 'alive', attested as TM MM ilínde, KM íllende, KP ilindé: dialectal variation or simply arbitrary accentuation?). Therefore the description of stress in the Mator language – if such a description is possible at all – remains a task for future research.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mator is extinct and known only from 18th–early-19th-c. word lists; the accent marks in Mueller's and Pallas's records fluctuate so much (same word marked on 2nd, 1st, and final syllable in different lists) that Helimski declines to state a stress rule. His earlier 1993 sketch (Jazyki mira, pp. 374–375) tentatively read the same marks as suggesting free, paradigmatically mobile stress gravitating to the first and the penultimate syllable, again with the caveat that the many fluctuations hamper analysis. Net: stress position not determinable from the sources; no tone information.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the illustrative triple ilínde / íllende / ilindé 'alive' showing inconsistent marking across the Taigi/Mator (Mueller), Karagas (Mueller) and Karagas (Pallas) lists.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern accent marks on isolated citation forms in historical word lists (Mueller 1730s–40s, Pallas 1780s); no phrase-level data exist.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Helimski sources describe the extinct Mator-Taigi-Karagas language (mato1250) as a whole, reconstructed from 18th–early-19th-century word lists (Mueller, Pallas, Spasskij); dialect sigla in the examples: M = Mator, T = Taigi, K = Karagas (the Samoyedic 'Karagas', not the Turkic Karagas/Tofa). No dialect-specific stress statement is made.

sources.note: Section 1.5.16 'Akzentzeichen und Betonung' (p. 133): Mueller accented all polysyllabic words and Pallas often marked word stress, but the notation fluctuates so strongly (e.g. 'lebendig' recorded as TM MM ilínde, KM íllende, KP ilindé) that even using these data is problematic; a description of Mator stress, if possible at all, remains a task for future research. Elsewhere (1.4, p. 109) non-first-syllable vowel reduction is noted, with a remark that blocking of reduction 'möglicherweise.. von den ursprünglichen Akzentverhältnissen abhängig' was.
